utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Before we commence, it will be necessary tomorrow to adjourn at 12.15 because all Judges are meeting in a Plenary session from 12.30. So it will not be possible to have the third session tomorrow morning. And could I mention that it has just been advised late on Friday by the Dutch security personnel that this whole area, including this building, will not be open at all to the public on Tuesday, the 31st of March, that is Tuesday week, the reason for that is an international conference at the highest government levels on Afghanistan which will be held in the adjoining building, the conference centre, so that this whole geographic area will be closed to the public which means we will not be able to enter or leave this building on Tuesday, the 31st of March. So in your planning ahead, if counsel can take account of the fact that tomorrow we must finish at 12.15 and that we will not be able to sit at all on Tuesday, the 31st of March. Mr. Stamp, I understand you have a matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It would be a matter that asks that we go in private session. Perhaps before we do that may I indicate it is in respect to protected measures for a witness to come. I rise because I think I should indicate to the Court that the application is -- we propose to make an application, but perhaps it might be better if the application is made when the witness -- just before the witness comes instead of breaking the flow of this witness. But I just wanted to say so at the first opportunity because we will have the information on the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will wait until this witness is to come. He is the witness following this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Following this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As it pleases you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will then have the witness that is to continue today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I remind you that the affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Baraybar. This afternoon I'm going to continue my cross-examination from where we broke off. It has to do with the statement you gave during your direct examination. Mr. Baraybar, I would like to ask you about wounds and the nature of the wounds established by your team. I wish to restrict myself only to the bodies that had been exhumed and then repatriated to Kosovo from Batajnica, Petrovo Selo, and in relation to the type of injury and kind of injury sustained by the persons on whose -- on whom autopsies had been carried out. We have here a document of yours that has already been admitted. We see in Batajnica that there was a total of 744 bodies. For 506, the cause of death was established, and the cause of death is unknown for 238 bodies. Now, my question: Your conclusion when speaking about this was that the persons who lost their lives were civilians in your view -- or rather, if they were not civilians, then they were persons who could not defend themselves. Why? Because they had bullet wounds rather than shrapnel wounds, and it is your experience that they are mainly the cause of death of persons who take part in combat. Could you please explain this to us. Where do you get this experience from, and what is it based on?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. What I said is that after carrying out a survey of some 25 armed conflicts, some of this information as a matter of fact was also submitted to the Court in the case of the Prosecutor against Brdjanin and Talic. The primary cause of morbidity and/or mortality in a traditional armed conflict, and by this I mean two groups of people fighting one other, armed both of them, whether it be guerillas, an army, or whatever, people with arms; generally the first cause of mortality and morbidity is shrapnel followed by gun-shots, that is in terms of mechanism of injury. When in these settings gun-fire is the leading cause as it may be, the distributions of injuries in the bodies are: The extremities, be arms and legs; thorax; and head. However, we have observed the reverse pattern in cases in which the context in which these people are dying is not an armed conflict as such, meaning that one of the groups is armed and the other one is not armed. So it is not a military engagement of some kind. In this case what we have recorded is that the distribution of injuries by gun-fire would be head, thorax, and extremities. In some cases, the number of injuries on the head and the thorax may be the same or very close one another. As in our case, for example, the thorax is slightly higher than the head but the head is extremely high for what it is. What I have also said is that -- and I can give you the quote. If you wish. Maybe if you wish you can tell me and I will give you the quote. It has been determined that in gun-fire contexts, meaning shoot-out context of some kind, some people may show skeletal injuries while other people may not show skeletal injuries. However, all of them may have died of gun-shots. When dealing with decomposed remains with all that remains, even if I'm being redundant here, is the skeleton or the bones, it is possible to assume that some of the remains that do not show any bone trauma may have also been injured by gun-fire not affecting bones, such as, for example, somebody being shot through the abdomen or through any other part of soft tissue through the body. I don't know whether I'm answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you can give me a particular quotation. What was it that you meant?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the quotation I was referring to was a quotation of how the context, in this case a gun-fire context, is the one that may determine a certain distribution of skeletal injuries in some cases and no skeletal injuries in some others. And the article I was referring to is by -- I will pronounce it and then spell it, De La Grand Maison, in French, so it would be D-e L-a G-r-a-n-d M-a-i-s-o-n, and associates 2001. I have the full -- the actual full quote in the bibliography of the report that has been already tendered to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, could you please tell me whether you are familiar with the autopsy reports of the soldiers of the Army of Yugoslavia and the policemen of Yugoslavia who lost their lives in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would depend. I mean, your question is quite -- I mean, broad. I mean, I have seen some reports primarily, if I'm not mistaken, on some cases. I'm just trying to recall now on what cases. On some specific cases of people we identified back -- back in Kosovo as belonging to possible soldiers, but unless you are more precise I cannot really give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking about the members of the police, and what I'm asking about the members of the military - at that time it was still definitely the territory of the sovereign Republic of Serbia in the sovereign Federal Republic of Yugoslavia - so I'm asking you about the members of the police and the Army of Yugoslavia who took part in fighting in Kosovo. Do you have any knowledge about that or not, in relation to autopsies, of course?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- no, in those cases you are mentioning, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the reports that you provided to the OTP, and some of them were admitted into evidence here, it appears that the number of cases that were solved while you headed the team was 1800, or rather, 1800 or 1900 cases from the territory of Kosovo. So did you make any comparative statistics in terms of bodies that you dealt with excluding Batajnica, Petrovo Selo, and Perucac?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we please have a reference to the passage that my learned colleague is calling -- is citing to where this number is referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you assist, please, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, right now I cannot give you a reference but I'm going to rephrase my question in that case. I'm going to ask Mr. Baraybar: How many exhumed bodies were autopsied, excluding Batajnica, Petrovo Selo, and Perucac, while he headed the organisation, that is. What I mentioned is contained in his report. I don't have the reference right now, so in order not to waste any time I've rephrased my question this way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not give you an exact number. I mean we could obviously extrapolate something on the consolidated list of missing persons. Meaning, I left in May -- the 1st of May, 2007, and the list you have here is April 2008, and before that you got another list of October 2006. Just for simplicity's sake, let's take the list of October 2006, in which 3.011 cases were closed, of which the ones that were examined, meaning remains were identified and therefore were subject of an examination, were 1751 plus 91. We could do a bit of an addition, if you wish, just to give you an exact number, would be 1842 remains. So I would say that that is the average number of cases that my office while directing that office examined -- I mean physically examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: As for the autopsies that were carried out, was cause of death established for those persons, and do you have these statistics as you did for Batajnica, Petrovo Selo, and Perucac, do you have those statistics? I'm asking you because I haven't seen them.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have them, and as far as I know they are not part of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this for the sake of the objectivity of your report in relation to your conclusion that the persons who were exhumed from Batajnica, Petrovo Selo, and by Lake Perucac were injured in a way that made it obvious that they could not defend themselves and that they were therefore unarmed persons. You referred to certain sources, and I see that these sources are French, French authors. I don't know what armed conflict and what part of the world you were actually dealing with. Do you know any research in relation to the conflict in Kosovo? Do you have any comparative study in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No; however, in my report tendered to the Court for the case of Brdjanin/Talic and then expanded also in an article by myself and Gasior, G-a-s-i-o-r, from 2006, it's a peer reviewed paper at the Journal of Forensic Sciences. We expand and explicit some of the resources you're referring to, not specifically regarding Kosovo but elsewhere in the Balkans, primarily Croatia and Bosnia, if I'm not mistaken, Croatia for certain; meaning, distribution of injuries by anatomical location, and the nature of injuries caused by one or another mechanism in wartime. But to answer your question: No, I have no sources for Kosovo, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, I was not challenging the part of the skeleton where the wounds were found or whatever it was that you did. I'm saying something else. You say that this indicates that these were unarmed persons who could not take part in combat, or if they were combatants they had no weapons at that moment. That's why I'm asking you whether you have any comparative knowledge from Kosovo in relation to the way in which war fair was waged, what weapons were used, and to what extent it was possible in view of traditional war conflicts, as you said, that injuries in combat can be sustained in the way in which you describe this, namely, coming from shrapnel and not being exit/entry wounds. That is the essence of my question. Do you have information about how conflicts in Kosovo developed in view of this assertion that you're making?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I have to -- I'm afraid I cannot tell you yes or no, but let's just put the thing in context. I have the conclusion of my report here. What it says: "Strongly suggesting the killing of individuals unable to defend themselves rather than the confrontation between two armed groups," suggesting, so I'm not affirming it. The information I have provided in this report and in the previous quotes I gave you is totally comparable to any other country in the world where different types of "war" have been waged. The survey of 25 armed conflicts from Cambodia to Afghanistan to the Balkans shows you various different kinds of contexts in which war has been waged and the pattern repeats itself in any place. To give you yet another example, this distribution of injuries, whether shrapnel first, gun-shot second, and when gun-shot having this specific pattern has been recorded in a killing in Peru dating from 1984 where a counter-insurgency war had been waged by the army. So again we may say what is the point of comparing Peru and Kosovo or Croatia or Bosnia, whatever, but it seems to be a quite universal thing. That is what we know for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right if I say after this response of yours that it is your conclusion that that is probably the way it was. You're not saying anything with 100 per cent certainty, are you, as regards whether they could or could not have defended themselves?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, because all the affirmations that an expert, such as myself or any other expert, would give you are the most probable scenarios not the most possible scenarios since we know that everything is possible 50/50 per cent. So the most probable scenario meaning that the evidence I have collected allows me to reconstruct this as a probability, but certainly I cannot give you a statistical probability because it is not the nature of the material we are working with to tell you this is probable 99.9 per cent. This is not DNA. Certainly we are not talking about that kind of quantitative variables, if you wish. But it is the most probable scenario. That is what an expert will reconstruct. The most probable scenario, not the most possible one, but the most probable one. Therefore, if I was certain to a hundred per cent that I am not. I mean, I'm not saying I'm a hundred per cent sure. I think this is the most probable scenario, meaning all these elements most likely assist us to conclude this, this is the most likely scenario; otherwise I would say that these attest to the killing of individuals unable to defend themselves. I said "strongly suggesting," so it is the most probable scenario. The information we have as compared with all the sets of information and as explained in this report lead us to conclude that, as the most likely cause. Now, is it possible that some other cause may have come into play here? Yes, it is possible. Everything is possible, but I cannot comment upon possibilities. I can only comment upon probabilities, the ones contained in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: However, had you had comparative data to show the Trial Chamber and the OTP as regards other persons whose bodies you looked at in Kosovo, and if you had very specific information, as you did for Batajnica, Petrovo Selo, and Perucac, you will agree with me that in that case, had we had these statistics, the probability of your assertions would have been much higher or perhaps it would have been non-existent. Had you showed us that the other bodies that you had examined had sustained injuries from shrapnel and then you say they probably lost their lives in armed conflict, the situation would be quite different. If all the bodies that you examined had only exit/entry wounds, as in gun-shot wounds. Will you agree with what I said just now?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't, but I'll tell you why. I mean, I'm not trying to disagree with you for the sake of keeping my argument, but there is a reason why I do disagree with you. Let's remember that the three mass graves which remains are discussed in this report correspond to specific events. These are not random people that end up in holes with other people. For example - and that is just out of pure recollection from my days in Kosovo - one of the groups of people came from Izbica and Izbica was a specific attack in a specific day when a number of people, not everybody, were killed. Other people came from Meja and in Meja it was another specific attack, so another event. Therefore, the event and the nature of the event is the one that will determine the nature of the injuries sustained by the victims because the event is an event of this kind or the other kind. Therefore, I cannot compare simply 1800, whatever number I gave you, 1842, I think, individuals found in Kosovo in various events to these events. Of course I can compare similar things. I can compare an event similar to Meja or to Izbica or whatever to another event of its kind, but I cannot compare all the bodies found in Kosovo that could be a collection of various events and various mechanisms and all the rest of it. For example, I cannot compare some old lady found dead in her apartment with Meja or something of the kind. I mean, it doesn't make any sense. Therefore, that's why I disagree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I would have agreed with you if you had written that in your report, but it's missing in your report. What we have in your report is a heap of death certificates and then forensic inspection reports, and I'll come back to one of these. It's Ba012 case that you had commented upon earlier in your testimony. Now let me see, I have a reference here. Just a minute. In B/C/S the report is 2794, 02794 is the English version, the certificate for Lirije Berisha and the forensic inspection report comes with it. We can see that on the screen. Right. I'm looking at this report. Why is the autopsy report only a few sentences long, and how are we who are interested -- I see Ms. Kravetz is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted to request a page reference to which page we are referring to in the report, if my learned colleague could kindly indicate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, Your Honour. I'll continue, and I'll give you the reference in due course. I'm asking a general question using this specific example because that's the one chosen by Mr. Baraybar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Why are all autopsy reports only a few sentences long; and how are we who are interested in the nature of injuries, the origin, the mechanism of the injury able to check these reports with our expert witnesses when the reports are so short and lacking in the kind of detail that we feel should be included so that we could review them critically? We have no minutes of the autopsy, no record of what had been established, the origin of the fractures, whether the injuries were post mortem or ante mortem? Why are the reports so short? Is that the usual practice?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. As a matter of clarity, what I have in front of me here is just the cover page of my report. Mr. Djordjevic was referring to, I think, the inspection report that I do not have it in front of me. I mean, I have the paragraph on page 11 of my report, but I don't think that is what he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Sure, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not to waste time, I would kindly ask the usher to give the witness a hard copy of the report that he discussed yesterday, and in the meantime we'll find a reference. I'll just ask the usher to show it to the Prosecutor first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. As I explained at the beginning of the examination, the forensic inspection, although the factor becomes a second autopsy, it is not a formal autopsy in that respect. Therefore, the information is quite summarised. However - now I have it here, yes - this doesn't mean that this document was produced in the autopsy room, certainly not. All the forms, the original forms, that were filled in by hand during the examination where they described each of the injuries and all the rest of it does exist. This piece of paper is only the forensic inspection report, as it says, which is a summary; it is not the paperwork that goes with it. Having said that, the forensic inspection is only that, an inspection, it is not a full autopsy in the way that was carried out in the -- in Serbia prior to transfer of the bodies. However, a lot of attention was given to reconstructing body parts that were broken in order to make these interpretations such as, for example, here gun-shot injury to the head, et cetera, describing the keyhole, where it is located, et cetera. But yes, I mean, there is pictures that go with these inspection reports, there is handwritten notes that go with them. I mean, all that does exists to my knowledge. It should be in the Office of Missing Persons in Kosovo. So all I'm trying to say is this piece of paper is not an examination. I was not in front of the body-bag and filled it in. This is only a summary that is produced for purposes such as this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: These are documents --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second one is P5148 and the first one -- let me repeat. P4556 and P5148.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My next question, Mr. Baraybar: To what extent did you take into account the autopsy reports of bodies repatriated to Kosovo from Batajnica, Petrovo Selo, and finally Perucac?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more precise in -- I mean, how -- if we took it --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you take them into account? Did you review them? Did you use them in your paper? Or did you not use them in your paper at all?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did. As a matter of fact, the whole issue of the forensic inspection comes after reviewing the first cases we received -- not the first eight, but when we were receiving a larger number of cases when you could actually see that they -- all of them, at least in Batajnica or Perucac, had cause of death ascertained; and it seemed that there had been like a cut and paste in the text, meaning that all were crushed by blunt-force instrument, cause of death was unascertained because the bodies were too decomposed. And obviously what was more worrying is that in some of the cases we found extra body parts. We found another arm or leg of another person that -- obviously there's nobody with three legs, and this was really a problem. Therefore, at some point we had a look at these reports but just as a reference -- as a reference. I mean, obviously the inspection report is still independent report, it's not -- we were not trying to pick, if you wish, "pick" on the mistakes of the others, but we had a duty towards the family -- there were a tremendous amount of pressure to hand over the remains, and we could not just hand over remains primarily if there were extra remains in the bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll go back to the statistics that you provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's 02795 in B/C/S, that's page 5455, that's -- sorry, it's P5455. Could we have that on the screen. I'm mostly interested in the table. The number is 5455. That's Exhibit 5455.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, P455 is on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the table you made for Batajnica. You have 238 unknown causes of death. What is the main reason why your team was unable to determine the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to clarify, I do not know whether it is a translation term. Unascertained is not the same thing that unknown, so this is cause of death unascertained; meaning that you are able to ascertain the most probable cause of death based on hard evidence that the body, so to speak, is providing you or the skeleton is providing you. You may have a skeleton of somebody who has been, let's say, poisoned, choked with a pillow or simply stabbed in soft parts of the abdomen and has no boney injuries of any kind. Therefore, you cannot ascertain the cause of death. It is not that it is unknown, but it is unascertainable, so to speak. So the reason, to answer your question, why these cases are unascertainable is because they were too fragmented or incomplete. As I told you, for example, there were some body-bags that contained more than one individual and, for example, you may have a torso that was articulated to arms and head and all the rest of it. But, for example, the legs, one leg may be his leg but the other leg could be somebody else's; or you may have only one leg and obviously you cannot ascertain the cause of death of a body based on a leg. Certainly you can assume certain things that if they take your leg you will die, but obviously that will be far too much far-fetched in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What does the number 238 unascertained mean? Because after your answer I'm completely at a loss. You have statistics where you say the number of cases, the number of ascertained causes of death, and this number is unascertained. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I already explained you, but I can say it again. From a total number of 744 individuals that you have, 506 had the cause of death ascertained based on physical evidence of the bodies themselves, while 238, the remaining of the 744, the cause of death could not be ascertained based on the remains we had examined. So, for example, there were incomplete remains, for example, there were skeletons with no injuries of any kind and things of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now I understand. I did not understand the previous answer quite clearly, but now you've made it quite clear. Now, my next question relating to these persons where the cause of death was not ascertained: Did I understand correctly that in Batajnica you found mostly skeletons with barely any tissue on them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that in case of a stab wound or an entry and exit wound through a tissue, you would have been unable to find a bullet wound and you were unable to say that the cause of death is a bullet wound?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, my next question: Would injuries sustained not only from a blade or a gun-shot also leave no trace on the skeleton?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I have another question concerning your report, D002-4164. I believe that's the version in English. It's over 50 pages long, so I won't call it up, but since you are the author I believe you are familiar enough. I want to look at the results of examination of human remains found in Berisa, Kosovo. You conducted the examination yourself, correct? Nine groups found in the location of Berisa, Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I am right, that was the evidence presented through the case of Limaj and others, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm giving you the exact number of the document. Let us call up the first page. D002-4166, to avoid any doubt. D002-4166.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is this something you have written yourself? Are you familiar with the document?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think on page 3 of this document it reads: "In the part of examination of wounds it says: "Due to the impossibility of determining whether the bullet wounds were post mortem or ante mortem, it was assumed that gun-shot wounds were the cause of death and occurred at the time of death ..." Is this forensic determination based on assumptions or on fact?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I will give you a lengthy answer because it requires a lengthy answer so we are all very clear regarding this. Forensic anthropologist, forensic pathologist, anybody examining extremely decomposed remains is determining the most probable cause of death, not the mechanism of death, unlike a pathologist working on a cadaver. For example, somebody has been shot to the head in a homicide, the cause of death definitely will be the gun-shot wound to the head. The mechanism of death, however, may be hypovolemic shock, I mean, the person bled to death or any other more pathophysiological mechanism. So what happens when you have a remain, a set of remains, that has no soft tissues of any kind; be bones, be something very decomposed? If we as scientists are trying to determine the mechanism of death of that individual, then we shouldn't even be in this court today, I mean there's no point of any examination. Because all you can say is that this body has a gun-shot wound to the head; however, I do not know whether the person was clinically dead or alive. I cannot say that the person -- when the person saw the gun had a heart attack and died. The question is: Is this logic a useful logic for any type of context? It isn't, in my opinion certainly, and it is an opinion I defend strongly. So I think that one of the things we have a take into account when dealing with this nature of cases, be extra-judicial killings, full disappearances, any kind of human rights violation, to put it in a broader sense. We have to take into account two things. One is the context, for example. The bodies found in these mass graves, these people did not go there themselves. These people did not bury themselves. A person found in a grave with a blindfold and hands tied behind the back is not a case of suicide. All I'm trying to say is that the context is defining a number of elements that you will find eventually on the body; by the same token when examining the remains and using that context into account you have to make that assumption - and yes it is an assumption - in absolute terms if we become the most purest of the purest certainly you cannot say if the person was clinically dead or alive. We can go into a metaphysical discussion as to what is alive or dead. Maybe the person got into a cataleptic state but was breathing or was no breathing or was no pulse but was this person alive or not? And use that hard evidence you are finding as an element that contributed to the cause of death not to the mechanism of death of the person. By the same token I will tell you: You find a body with five shots through the head, if the person was dead, why did you shoot the person five times in the head? Of course they can give you an answer, anybody can give you an answer. This explanation I gave you refers to the need for determining the most probable cause of death. This also means there has to be some correlates between the injuries you are describing in real life as I mention in this report in the paragraph -- last paragraph, I refer, for example, to some paper by Okoye and Kimmerle in the year 2000 where they were looking, for example, at patterns of activity and survival of people after they were shot. So, for example, you know somebody shot on the head likely will die or will die after very few minutes depending on what calibre of weapon this person was shot, certainly. While somebody shot with a rifle through the thorax or the chest would also eventually die. And this person may run for 2 metres or 10 metres and then drop dead. So all these studies help you to relate the physical injuries you are recording in this bone in this decomposing body to a specific clinical correlate that physicians and other people deal with on a daily basis. So what is actually written here has also been written and peer reviewed certainly in other publications I can provide you if you are interested that is called, On the means of determining the most probable cause of death; and that is something that is quite generally assumed as a -- I mean procedure in any setting, I mean not only in this Tribunal but in any setting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, is it in the purview of an anthropologist to establish the origin of injuries of bones, the mechanism of their occurrence in determining the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, meaning the anthropologist assist the pathologist in ascertaining the most probable cause of death, as I already explain you. And definitely it is in the purview of the anthropologist to determine the mechanism of injury because we work with bones, and if it's not us who would do it? A pathologist deals with soft tissues, with organs and tissues. I mean, we work with bones. Bones is are our subject of study, so to speak, so we have to understand how a bone breaks, how a bone grows. We need to know everything about bones, and yes -- the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about the mechanism of the occurrence of injuries, of the infliction of injuries, would that be included too?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I mean, as I explain you -- I mean, even as an anthropologist if I cannot differentiate between a hole in the bone caused by a gun or caused by a drilling machine, then I would be jobless I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Again on page 3 of the same report we read that all the entry and exit wounds in the area of the head and chest are lethal, or is it my misunderstanding? Would you confirm this? Would you say that all gun-shot wounds to the chest and the head are lethal?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to take this comment in the context in which it has been written. When determining the most probable cause of death, you have two kinds of injuries, okay. The first kind of injury called lethal are injuries limited to the head and the torso, the thorax, and lethal if untreated could be injuries linked to the arm -- I mean to the arm and to the leg, primarily the thigh and the upper arm, primarily because of the link between the comminution or the fracturing of the humerus, I mean the bone of the arm, and the femur, that is the bone of the thigh, and the presence of the arteries, brachial artery in the arm and the femoral artery on the leg, that normally lacerated at the time of a high velocity through those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, have you heard of the Baraybar collection? Does the term mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most definitely. I mean, I have certainly heard about the Baraybar collection, not that it exists, but yes I have certainly heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Baraybar forensic skeletal collection, right? Can you tell me what that is?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the term was given I guess by those who gave or named this so-called collection after me were trying to honour me, although they didn't really make my life easier as a matter of fact. ICTY had or the Office of the Prosecutor had a project through the work they did in Bosnia, primarily Bosnia, and Kosovo in order to re-calculate aging standards for Balkan populations and that is what was done. The papers with peer reviewed and published last year, in 2008, I think the Journal of Forensic Sciences. This "collection" consisted of a number of sleeves of bone and casts and -- I know that after this collection -- or these bones, sorry, I mean, were used for these examinations and then returned to -- returned from wherever they came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That collection of bones it was made by whom? Why is it named after you?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I was the resident forensic scientist in the Tribunal, and I was acting as chief anthropologist in most of these occasions, I oversaw this project; and that is why I believe these scholars at the University of Tennessee, in the United States, who carried out the work, thought that there would be really a distinction, if you wish, to call these series of studies - because there's no, as far as I know, physical collection of bones behind some glass windows - after me. That is, I mean, my understanding of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you attend the meeting, professional meeting, of anthropologists, pathologists, forensic scientists of the American Academy for Forensic Science in Dallas 2004 when Tennessee university researchers presented this entire project? Were you present, and could you tell us, if you were there, what you remember from that occasion, from that congress?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there, and I remember I arrived late and I gave a paper that is -- that has been published within the same volume of that symposium that is called: When there is no DNA can we still identify people? It is published within that symposium in 2008, if I'm not mistaken, I mean the publication in the Journal of Forensic Sciences and, as a matter of fact, I did learn then that when the symposium was introduced, I have been given the honour, if you wish, to have this "collection" named after me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't it different over there -- wasn't it a fact that you and the entire group of scholars from Tennessee were exposed to serious criticism in view of the ethnic background of the entire story, and also all the bones of these victims were obtained by you without the consent of their next of kin and no one had been informed about that. At that time Mr. Graham Blewitt Deputy Prosecutor of the OTP said that you were authorised to carry out an investigation, but that was in the broadest possible terms; whereas the scientists from Tennessee said that they did not know that these bones or remains were from the victims from Kosovo and Bosnia. Am I right if I say that you and the entire team were exposed to severe criticism by a professor of anatomy and forensic anthropology and other scientists who attended the gathering? Therefore, the entire project was brought into question?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is an opinion. I can explain you this. If it was anybody that has been subject of much heated debate -- and I'm being very politically correct, not to say slandering - has been actually myself. And as you well know if you go to internet and just type my name and put bones next to it and it will have quite a lot of articles and comments of otherwise unnamed scientists criticising this and that and the only name that is associated to that is mine. So far, I have not seen any scholarly disagreement or discussion regarding these series of papers that have been published, as I said, and peer reviewed. And that is exactly the type of criticism I would pretty much expect. All the other type of criticism that actually started with a publication in the Sunday -- what was it -- no sorry, it was the Sydney herald back in 2001, if I'm not mistaken, and some obscure magazine in the United Kingdom called The Age, and I remember this because I was working for the Tribunal in Sanski Most I think. You know, the same -- the same topic pretty much with various different backgrounds came over and over and over over the years. And it seems there's still -- I mean, moves quite a lot of people and gives a lot of inspiration to a lot of people to keep writing about this. But regarding that I have no comments. This type of work is not a popularity contest. Therefore, I am not searching whatever is written about myself on a daily basis, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us your comments with regard to the statements made by your colleagues from the University of Tennessee who said that they were not aware of the origins of these bones and they found out only later that the bones had come from recently deceased persons, or rather, the way you put it, recently killed persons. Why was it that you said that, or rather, that they said that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- this is the first time I heard about my colleagues from Tennessee saying such a thing. So maybe you provided me the quote in what newspaper it has been said -- I mean, in any case, even if I see it, I have nothing to comment. If it is true they say that, well, you should ask yourself to them. I mean, I have nothing to comment on that. This is the first time I hear it in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You were asked by journalist from an organisation that is called IACAN [as interpreted], Kosovo Action Network. The journalist is Petra Kirning [phoen] and Kees Birning [phoen] you said the same thing that they should be asked why they had stated that, but that's not really the most important thing that we're dealing with now. I'm interested in the following: Why were samples taken for 800 bodies? Was it to establish the possible age of the persons who were supposed to meet the requirements of a profile of a Kosovar or Bosniak? I think that's what you said. Was that the reason of the scientific research, to establish the possible age of the deceased person after the skeletons were found? Was that the reason why the bones were taken? As far as I know, it was the ribs and the collar bones that were taken; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has been put a compound question. There are several questions in fact in this one question. He also hasn't been shown the source of the materials my learned colleague is talking about. So I wonder if we could first break up the question and also if the witness could be directed to the source of the -- of this allegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are presented with compound questions and compound objections. If you want the witness to comment with some intelligence, it will be necessary to put to him the article and the specific reference. The way you're putting it, I would suggest, would preclude the witness from bringing any sort of sensible expertise to an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, then it's going to take a bit longer because I familiarised myself with this material just before the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So first of all, for the purposes of your research, did you take the remains of the bones of over 800 corpses or not? There.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, it was not my research, as I already said; and second, I do not know on the top of my head how many remains or samples of remains were taken, but the number may be correct -- actually, you have -- you got the source, I don't have it. So I would say or consider that is the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to answer whether it's possible or whether it is a number that is just that big. At whose proposal was this project started, the taking of these bones, and what was the purpose of the taking of these bones because we heard that you did take bones --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're now getting into multiple questions, multiple questions again. Now, do you want the witness to comment on a specific article?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right. You are right, Your Honour. I don't want the witness to say anything about any article because it may be a case of libel or slander. I'm asking him whether it is correct that they took the remains of bones of over 800 corpses and the witness said that that is possible. And now I'm asking under whose supervision and at whose proposal were these samples taken. He was the head then so I'm asking whether it was his proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Let him answer that then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said at the beginning, the proposal to the Office of the Prosecutor, the scientific concept of that was mine although it was not my personal research, collection, whatever else we want to add. And just to answer now, since we are at it, your compound question, I mean the other two parts of your question is the why, the reason why, is very simple. Over the years in the Balkans, the standards for determining age, individual age, skeletal age that has been used were primarily derived from American -- North American populations. What we now know is that different populations age skeletal-wise, obviously, I'm not talking about whether somebody's wrinkled or not, in different ways. Therefore, in order to be objective not just when you reconstruct demographic profiles, meaning you got so many people dying between, let's say, 25 and 35 or something of the kind; but also to assist with individual identification, meaning I suspect this person was so and so and part of his profile is that it is a male and is this age requires to have age standards that are derived from that population in question. That is why now one of the things or one of the objectives of forensic anthropologists throughout the world is to elaborate what is called population-specific standards. I cannot use an African standard and apply on a South American population or North American standard and use it in any other thing. So that is the reason. I do not know whether it is clear, but that is the -- I mean, the overall reason. I mean, I can obviously expand, but, I mean, I don't know if you're satisfied with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In part. My next question in relation to this collection, this bone collection: I've read this and now you're going to tell me whether it's correct or not. In several articles of that, not at one, that the samples that had been taken were the pubic bone, rib, and collar bone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is and it isn't. Depending -- let's see. In the clavicle, they took a piece of the clavicle for what is called osteon counting, that is a histological technique, as a matter of fact, that requires a slight of bone so not the whole bone, that's one thing. The second thing is, the pubic bone in some cases was resected and in some others cases was casted. So they took a cast, kind of like a silicone cast. And the ribs, the same thing, some where the external extremity, meaning the extremity that is closer to the cartilage was cut, that is a 2-centimetre or 3-centimetre cut or was casted as well. So it depends. It is a variation of this -- again, I do not have with me inventories or anything of the kind to tell you how many casts or how many actual specimens were taken, but this is variation and a combination of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The next question I would be interested in the remains of the bones that were taken from the remains of these bodies. Did this have to do with persons whose identity had been established or were these persons whose identity had not been established?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were a combination of both. There is a large number of cases with known identities and there are some other cases with unknown identities. The thing is that now, the standards derived from the known can be employed to the unknown. That is, in lay terms, what it is about, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke of the profile that you were interested in, did it have to do with the Balkans or the former Yugoslavia or, for example, only Kosovo and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess these were -- profile has been quoted from where? From an article? I mean, somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What you said yourself just a moment ago. You said that the profile of establishing the age of the remains could not be identical to the one used in North America and that's why you started the entire project. However, since you say that the research was in Kosovo and Bosnia, Yugoslavia, the former Yugoslavia, rather, is a broader notion and the Balkans is an even broader notion. So now I'm interested in hearing what the purpose of your investigation was. What area?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did not use the word profile, I used the word population-specific standard. And as a people, former Yugoslavia is a quite representative sample of a people. In other words, aging -- aging in former Yugoslavia will be much more uniform as a people are taken and as a population, no matter how we want to divide these populations up in subgroups than, for example, a North American population that yet again is a multi-racial population or is a multi-national population. So the idea was to create population-specific standard for that part of the Balkans that is quite representative as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, before you got this idea to do that, you mentioned the word standard rather than profile. Did you use European profiles or standards? Are you familiar with those standard? Why didn't you use them rather than American standards?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, and we're going to go into a very technical detail here, the only -- let's go back in time a bit. In 1995/1996 we were, for example, working in Rwanda, okay, not even in the Balkans but in Rwanda, and we have bodies to examine and we have to come up with a specific individual profiles in this case regarding how old they were, males or females and so on. Then the only forensic standards we did have at hand were the ones they were and widely used were North American standards. Why is that? The North American standards, and I'm referring to two specific standards here, one called the Suchey-Brooks that refers to the changes or metamorphosis of the pubic synthesis that is part of your pelvis to parts of your pelvic bones, and then the standards produced by Iscan and Loth based on the metamorphosis of the external end of the ribs were the only forensic standards available. Why were they the only forensic standards available? Because these people have actually carried out an identical research collecting autopsy room specimens of known age and sex. In the case of Suchey-Brooks was a very large multi-racial sample at Los Angeles county medical examiners office while the samples from Iscan and Loth were from Florida somewhere. But these were the only robust standards that could be applied in forensic contexts until then. So we came mid-1996 to the Balkans and yet again we had the same problems as in Rwanda, what standard should we use? Of course there were other standards, for example, the European association of anthropologists that has some kind of standards; but they were not forensic standards. They have been derived on medieval populations. Of course you have some other standards by Aksavi [phoen] and Nemeskedy [phoen] very famous Hungarian professors of anthropology that have developed the complex methods widely used in the Balkans and in this way. These cases yet again where is majority, archeological populations that cannot be compared to modern individuals. So if I had a choice in 1996 I have to use what I had at hand, but obviously the idea was that we have to be using something that could actually be replicated elsewhere and used by those who would continue the work of identification in the Balkans, I mean beyond ICTY, as they do it now. So that is the reason. So when we talk about standards we have to be very careful because, yes, there is a lot of standards. But the validity and the usability of a standard is only dependent upon the sample on which it was based and whether it is applicable or not in a medical-legal context. I cannot apply or for that matter even defend a report and say I have used, you know, standards derived from an Egyptian population from the time of the Pharaohs to apply to a Bosnian sample or Peruvian sample here. That doesn't really work. Here you're trying to defend the specific identify of one individual or a group of individuals so you have to really base your things on the most accurate things you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: How could you then provide findings for all these bodies -- or actually, tell me, when did the collection start, actually, the collection known as the Baraybar skeletal collection, what year?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The project, if I'm not mistaken, started back in -- this I would question, 1998 or 1999, one of those two years. Again, I'm using my own sort of memory, so to speak -- I mean the project -- I rather call the project rather than to my learned colleagues in Tennessee using the name or my name for the project.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: If it's 1998, when did Bosnia happen then? You said that remains were taken from Bosnia too, parts of skeletons, that is. Am I right or wrong on that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- yes. I mean, as I -- I think I already said it. This project contemplated things from -- remains from Bosnia, and there's a tiny collection, if I'm not mistaken, there's a tiny collection from Croatia as well and Kosovo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is that also 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yet again, based on my recollection, I think the project started in 1998 or 1999. I mean, then -- I don't have the -- I mean, I got nothing. I'm just using my own memory for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said that there were both identified and unidentified corpses from which these remains were taken. Tell me, in the case of the identified bodies, was consent sought officially from family members to take these bones for scientific research or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These bones were collected as part of the autopsy procedure. As in any autopsy you collect the specimens you need for your examination; and in these types of cases, the determination of age or whatever determination was part of the investigation of that specific case. If in an autopsy you collect tissue samples, you collect urine and blood and vitreous and organ samples, whatever you need, in order to conclude your case, there was the same logic. So there was not an issue of, I don't know, taking pieces for some strange, I mean, experiment of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, that's certainly not what I meant; however, I'm asking you this because of the feedback involved from the families of these victims and the representatives of certain international organisations that voiced their views on this. For example, Mrs. Munira Subasic, Mothers from Srebrenica and Zepa; then again a gentleman who spoke on behalf of Shpresimi [phoen] and Mari [phoen] Hoti, the Association of Missing Persons. Their comment was that this was scandalous, that no one had asked them about this, and that they are all appalled. I don't know whether you're aware of these comments or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm aware is that a number of very irresponsible journalists and maybe, maybe -- I would say maybe, although I'm almost sure, colleagues as a matter of fact unnamed so far decided that it was really a good venture to go to the media with these type of very inaccurate comments and then to the families to tell the families that indeed somebody has been taking pieces of the loved ones for some private collection, maybe a collection that I had in my house or under my bed or something like that, because I have heard that too; and the families therefore in -- reacted, as expected they would react, when exposed to this kind of information. What can I tell you? It has been -- I have lived through these types of slandering campaigns for years now. And they have used the families when the families, I mean, stopped saying whatever they have to say, they went back to the families again and when they did not hear anything from the families they invented something else and that. So there's quite a lot of those things on the internet. I stopped reading them, frankly. For my mental health I have stopped reading them a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have very few questions left, but I believe that the time is right for the technical break. I've already overstepped, but I'll have a maximum of ten minutes left for my questions for Mr. Baraybar, and I will then conclude my cross-examination. I think it would be a good idea to take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, a break now will enable you to look over your remaining notes and consolidate your thoughts, perhaps, Mr. Djordjevic. So we will adjourn now and resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Baraybar, my last question is related to this embarrassment connected to the bone collection. Did the collection remain at the University of Tennessee, or were the bones returned to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the University of Tennessee has returned all remains to ICTY. I mean, I no longer work for ICTY, as you know; therefore, questions regarding that should be addressed to the University of Tennessee. But as far as I know, bones were returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: One more question. Why were the bones taken to the USA in the first place, to the university?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The University of Tennessee is, I would say, the, with a capital T, university that has developed the most comprehensive forensic anthropology programme in the US among all other universities, as you may know, the department there was -- and the forensic anthropology programme was set up by Dr. William Bass, a very well-known forensic anthropologist. As a matter of fact, his -- one of his books is pretty much a textbook used by forensic anthropologists, I mean, all over the world. So that was the main reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was it at your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was my suggestion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any kind of understanding or a protocol between the ICTY and the University of Tennessee about this?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yet again, you should ask ICTY, but I presume there is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You personally, as head of the PMF, no nothing about this, about any sort of agreement or protocol?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say I know nothing, but as I told you you should actually ask ICTY because I stop working for ICTY in 2002. I understand there was some kind of agreement, but obviously I was not part of that agreement since I was not employed by that institution. I am not the right person, based on recollection, to answer anything related to that because it's just recollection. I do not know. I don't have any documents in front of me. But, I mean, I guess the right body to be asked would be the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is there an expert report at the University of Tennessee sent to the OTP or the Tribunal that has ever been used in a courtroom in any case before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yet again, you should ask the University of Tennessee they have sent a specific report to ICTY; however, there's a suite of papers published in the Journal of Forensic Sciences, peer reviewed papers that at least within the North American, more specifically United States system, would comply with the so-called Daubert standard of peer reviewed publications that can be used in court published last year, 2008, yet again I do not have with me the specific issue, but I can -- I think you can find it on internet without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking this because I suppose that the University of Tennessee received these fragments of bones in order to perform expert analysis for the benefit of a trial here or some other case, but I suppose you don't have any information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now can we call up 5453 [In English] -- that is the headline. [Interpretation] Page 18. [In English] It is not 5453, it is P, P453. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On the screen at the moment is I think Exhibit P455; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P5453 is the one we need -- sorry, P453, page 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, I'm interested in whether we need to receive the document on the screen as an exhibit. You referred to it when you were questioning the witness. It's a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not used this document at all, Your Honour. This is a protocol on forensic experts and reports, it's P453, it's a document I have not used before, P453, page 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, I don't think we are understanding each other. On your screen at the moment is a document you asked to be put on your screen which you referred to the witness. Do you want it to be received as an exhibit or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do want to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I tell you that you're in very good company, Mr. Djordjevic. Mr. Djurdjic has set the example for this. We will receive the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00064, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. May I kindly ask for the protocol on the exchange of forensic experts and reports to be shown on the screen. It's P453, page 18. That's correct. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Now a very short question. Are you familiar with this protocol?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did any cooperation actually take place under this protocol? And when I say that, I mean an exchange of your experience, the mutual exchange of experience between pathologists, anthropologists, or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in general terms, yes. I would say that we were very accommodating to Serbian forensic experts to come to Kosovo to oversee the exhumation and examination of any remains that they suspected to be non-Albanians. On the other hand, however, most of the, if not all, the exhumations and examinations of remains found in Serbia proper were carried out prior to my office being set up. Therefore, I was not even there, so we could not really -- I mean, be reciprocated, so to speak, in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: My question basically is this: Did you exchange data with Serbian experts regarding precisely what I call profile and you call standard, if I'm not mistaken, of the age of the exhumed bodies? Was there any cooperation on that issue and on the application of certain standards that were not familiar to you because you said that the Northern American standard was the one you applied beginning with Rwanda and former Yugoslavia and further on?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I already told you, the final publication of the standards, I mean as peer-review standards, has taken place last year. I left Kosovo the year before. Therefore, by definition, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So your answer is no. Thank you. I have no further questions. I thank you for the answers you've provided today and over the past three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my cross-examination. If any other comments arise, we will file a submission in writing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you wanting this document received as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Again [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's being pointed out by our court officer that it's already an exhibit, so you've done well. Ms. Kravetz, is there any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I have nothing in re-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Judge Baird has some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Baraybar, I shall like to take your mind back to the reference you made to the tangential gun-shot wound to the head, the keyhole, as you called it, displaying exit and entrance wounds simultaneously. Now, can you tell us what was or what would have been the position of the deceased in relation to the person doing the actual shooting?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a very tricky question, as a matter of fact, Your Honour, and is a question that is generally posed -- generally by lawyers, if I may say. One thing we have to understand regarding this is that the trajectories that are presented in a corpse, I mean in a skeleton, are in relation to the anatomical position of the individual, so irrespective of whether the person was, for example, lying or standing. Anatomically it would be standing with both arms extended next to the body. So in those absolute terms it would be from let's say back to front, above to below, below to above. However, in a case like this one I cannot tell you whether the person was with a head, for example, bent or kneeling or something. In very specific cases certain shots generally caused by handguns in this case can provide us more insights as to how the person may have been, I mean, placed in or regarding the person shooting. For example, shots that enter areas that are covered by the neck, in which you actually need for the head to be hyper-flexed, meaning flexed anteriorly, there is no other way by which the bullet could come in that way. But with high-velocity rounds such as in this case that's a high-velocity round, a rifle round, it is extremely difficult to say in what position the person was. I do not know whether I am answering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, you referred to the peri mortem injury. Now, a peri mortem injury is in essence a post mortem injury, is it not.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not, as a matter of fact. Peri mortem is distinguished by post mortem by the fact that it belongs to the interval around the time of death, meaning could be slightly before or slightly after. In other words, let's say I have a person, I shoot this person and the person dies of an injury, but let's assume that I shoot the person a second time and the person is clinically dead. I will not be able to find in that second interval a difference between the first and the second shot. The only way to find this out, and I may say there's an element of current research in various -- in various places, is on the detection of certain elements that are produced by your body while you are alive. For example, some by-products of blood -- of bleeding specifically more than of blood, but of bleeding -- certain proteins that may be produced when you are alive. Therefore, yes, if I shoot a dead body and the body bleeds because this person died 30 seconds ago, this person is not producing that substance. That would be a lay way to put it. But for the time being it has been for the last many many years, peri mortem is something we interpret as around the moment or the episode of the death. So it could be slightly before or, yes, slightly after. But post mortem is something more of an artefact. For example, I threw the body in a grave and then the massive rocks, I mean, covered the body and broke the bones, and things of the kind. That would be post mortem, but peri mortem is around the time of death.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: There is no line of demarcation between the peri mortem and -- there is none, I suppose, there is none.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, yet again, the beauty of somebody working with a cadaver is that having soft tissues you can actually measure that. You can measure the person bled because you have the blood, you've got the broken vessel because you've got a hematoma because you have everything. Not having that, as such as in bone, you remain with other things that are less precise, they may be as accurate as, but less precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I see. I thank you very much indeed, Dr. Baraybar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll be pleased to know that that concludes the questioning for you. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance for the assistance you've been able to give and the time that you've been asked to devote to this. We are grateful. You may of course now resume to your ordinary activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I may, can I say something? It's just, I had a note -- I have a note here on a clarification for Mr. Djordjevic, as a matter of fact, that I wanted to say as a closing remark of mine if I may steal some of the time of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would depend upon Mr. Djordjevic. Would you like to hear, Mr. Djordjevic? I take that as a yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Rather no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Okay. That's the answer, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stamp, we understand there's a matter you wish to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. If I could do so in private session, I'd be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
